mcqs.q: A complication of local anaesthesia is best defined as:
opts: Any deviation from the normally expected pattern during or after LA
mcqs.explain: A complication is any deviation from the normal expected result (loss of pain without adverse effects).

mcqs.q: A mild complication is distinguished from a severe one in that it:
mcqs.explain: A mild complication shows a slight change that reverses without specific treatment; a severe one is pronounced and requires definite treatment.

mcqs.q: Transient facial nerve paralysis after an IANB is caused by depositing LA into the:
opts: Parotid gland capsule (posterior border of the ramus)
mcqs.explain: LA introduced into the parotid gland capsule blocks the facial nerve (CN VII) during an IANB or Akinosi block.

mcqs.q: A patient with facial nerve paralysis after an injection typically cannot:
opts: Close the eye or control the lip on the affected side
mcqs.explain: Loss of motor function of the facial expression muscles means the patient cannot close the eye, blow the cheek or control the lip on that side.

mcqs.q: The key management step for facial nerve paralysis after LA is to:
opts: Reassure the patient and protect the eye from dryness
mcqs.explain: Management is reassurance plus protecting the eye from drying until the temporary paralysis resolves.

mcqs.q: Trismus following a local anaesthetic injection most often results from:
opts: Injection into muscle/ligament, needle-borne infection or a contaminated solution
mcqs.explain: Trismus can follow injection into muscles/ligaments, needle-borne infection or contaminated solution; treatment targets the cause plus exercise and analgesics.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised cause of pain during a local anaesthetic injection?
opts: A very cold or non-isotonic solution injected too rapidly
Slow injection of a warm solution
mcqs.explain: Pain causes include non-isotonic or very cold solution, too-rapid or contaminated injection, multiple punctures and injection into muscle/ligament.

mcqs.q: Infection following a local anaesthetic injection is usually due to:
opts: A non-sterile needle/solution or carrying bacteria into deeper tissue with the needle tip
mcqs.explain: Infection arises from non-sterile needles/solutions or carrying bacteria from the mucosa into deeper tissues with the needle tip.

mcqs.q: A haematoma after a local anaesthetic injection is:
opts: Effusion of blood into tissue from a punctured vessel
mcqs.explain: A haematoma is the effusion of blood into the tissues from a punctured vessel; haemoglobin breakdown then causes skin discoloration (ecchymosis).

mcqs.q: A haematoma is most commonly associated with which injection?
mcqs.explain: Haematoma is usually associated with the zygomatic/infraorbital (PSA) injection, where vessels (pterygoid plexus, maxillary artery) may be punctured.

mcqs.q: Management of a haematoma consists of:
opts: Pressure (if caught early) and cold application
mcqs.explain: Apply pressure (if noticed as bleeding begins) and cold; the haematoma fades gradually over days to weeks.

mcqs.q: Traumatic ulcers on the palate after LA are usually caused by:
opts: Injecting a large volume of solution
mcqs.explain: A large volume of LA injected into the dense palatal tissue can produce sloughing and traumatic ulceration.

mcqs.q: Self-inflicted lip/cheek injury after an IANB is most common in:
mcqs.explain: Children especially may chew the numb lip after an IANB, or the lip may be pinched between forceps and teeth, causing soft-tissue injury.

mcqs.q: Prolonged anaesthesia (paraesthesia) after an injection may be caused by:
opts: Needle trauma to the nerve or contamination by alcohol/germicide
mcqs.explain: Prolonged anaesthesia can follow contamination of the solution by alcohol/germicide or direct needle trauma to the nerve.

mcqs.q: Needle trauma to a nerve is typically signalled at the time of injection by:
opts: A sharp, 'hot' pain felt by the patient
mcqs.explain: Direct needle trauma to the nerve is felt as a sharp, hot, electric-like pain at the moment of injection.

mcqs.q: The management of prolonged anaesthesia from needle trauma is mainly to:
opts: Reassure the patient that it will resolve without treatment
mcqs.explain: Most cases resolve spontaneously, so reassurance of the patient is the key management step.

mcqs.q: Which practice helps PREVENT a broken needle?
opts: Never change the needle's direction while it is embedded — withdraw and redirect
Insert the needle fully to the hub
mcqs.explain: Prevent breakage by not forcing against resistance, not using too-fine a gauge, not redirecting an embedded needle, not inserting to the hub, and not surprising the patient.

mcqs.q: If a needle breaks and a fragment protrudes from the tissue, the operator should:
opts: Stay calm, keep the mouth open and grasp it with a hemostat
Push it deeper to hide it
Tell the patient to close immediately
mcqs.explain: Remain calm, keep the mouth open, and remove a protruding fragment with a hemostat; if nothing protrudes it must be removed surgically.

mcqs.q: The frequency of broken-needle complications has been greatly reduced by:
mcqs.explain: Disposable (single-use) needles, which are not weakened by re-sterilisation, have greatly reduced needle breakage.

saqs.q: Define a local complication of LA and distinguish mild from severe.
saqs.a: Any deviation from the normally expected pattern (loss of pain without adverse effects). Mild — slight change reversing without treatment; severe — pronounced, needing definite treatment.

saqs.q: Explain facial nerve paralysis after an IANB and its management.
saqs.a: LA enters the parotid gland capsule (posterior ramus) and blocks CN VII → the patient cannot close the eye/control the lip on that side. Management: reassure the patient and protect the eye from dryness.

saqs.q: List causes of pain during a local anaesthetic injection.
saqs.a: Non-isotonic or very cold solution, too-rapid injection, contaminated solution, multiple punctures, or injection into muscle/ligament.

saqs.q: Describe a haematoma: cause, common site and management.
saqs.a: Effusion of blood into tissue from a punctured vessel, usually with the zygomatic/infraorbital (PSA) injection; haemoglobin breakdown causes ecchymosis. Manage with pressure and cold; it fades over days/weeks.

saqs.q: How does soft-tissue sloughing/ulceration occur after LA?
saqs.a: Traumatic palatal ulcers from injecting a large volume of LA, and self-inflicted injury from chewing the numb lip after an IANB (children) or pinching the lip between forceps and teeth.

saqs.q: What causes prolonged anaesthesia, and how is it managed?
saqs.a: Caused by contamination with alcohol/germicide or needle trauma to the nerve (sharp 'hot' pain at injection). Management: reassurance — it usually resolves without treatment.

saqs.q: List measures to prevent a broken needle.
saqs.a: Don't force against resistance; don't use too-fine a gauge; don't redirect an embedded needle (withdraw first); don't insert to the hub; don't surprise the patient. If it breaks: retrieve a protruding part with a hemostat, else remove surgically.
